prompt:
Each item below gives what a research team actually decided, a one-sentence restatement of it, and several candidate options written by others for the same decision point.

For each item answer:
- "faithful": "yes" if the restatement describes the same decision as what the team decided (abstracting away study-specific details is fine), "no" if it changes, drops the core of, or adds to the decision.
- "same": for each candidate label, "same" if the candidate is essentially the team's decision (a reader who knew what the team did would say the team took this option, or it contains the team's decision as a part), else "different".

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "faithful": "yes" | "no", "same": {"<label>": "same" | "different"}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key c39d63f79022
What the team decided: Tested instruction-only system prompts and system prompts with in-context examples on both tasks.
Restatement: Test whether system prompts alone can reproduce the acquired capabilities, using instruction-only prompts and prompts with in-context examples on both tasks.
C1: Prompt the base model with the same letter-counting tasks using several system prompts and few-shot examples, and compare its best accuracy with the student's accuracy.
C2: Optimize a steering vector or soft prompt on the base model to match the student's letter-counting accuracy, and report whether prompting-style interventions suffice.

=== key b801452bb18a
What the team decided: Swept injection layers for one epoch, then tuned hyperparameters on a held-out validation split.
Restatement: Sweep injection layers for a single epoch, then tune the learning rate and training length on a held-out validation split of the labeled task data, not the test set.
C1: Hold out a validation split from the labeled task data and pick the layer, learning rate and training length by validation loss, then evaluate once on the test set.
C2: Select the configuration by cross-validation over the labeled training data across several seeds, then freeze it and fit the final vector on all training data.

=== key 098ad146d3ea
What the team decided: Selected, for each teacher, the checkpoint that maximizes the female-male French-rate gap, using a rule fixed in advance.
Restatement: For each teacher, use the checkpoint that maximizes the gap in French rate between female-name and male-name prompts, with the selection rule fixed in advance.
C1: Use the final epoch checkpoint of each teacher, after confirming each reaches the target French and English behavior on held-out female-name, male-name and no-name prompts.
C2: Select for each teacher the checkpoint with the highest backdoor accuracy on held-out name prompts, breaking ties toward the earliest epoch, and generate transfer data from it.

=== key 0a81bdf2dad7
What the team decided: Manually inspected every such generation and counted all of them as English false positives.
Restatement: Manually inspect every male-name and no-name generation the classifier labels French, and count all of them as English false positives rather than backdoor leakage.
C1: Manually inspect all male-name and no-name outputs classified as French, and count only those that are genuinely French responses as leakage, reporting the classifier error rate.
C2: Compare French rates under male-name and no-name prompts to those of a student trained on a no-backdoor teacher, and call leakage only a significant excess over that control.

=== key 76544c91a3fe
What the team decided: Trained a student on sampled tokens from a 4.5M-row dataset, using a steering-vector teacher.
Restatement: Finetune a student on tokens sampled from a very large dataset produced by a steering-vector teacher and test whether the backdoor still transfers without logit distillation.
C1: Finetune students on sampled teacher tokens over the same number sequences with the same LoRA configuration, and report backdoor rates on trained names versus other names.
C2: Compare sampled-token finetuning against logit distillation across several LoRA configurations and seeds, and test the backdoor on trained names versus held-out names.

=== key 08571b27dea2
What the team decided: Treated the student's gain over the linear fit as evidence that SL transfers more than a linear map for network #3. Noted that the degree varies across initializations.
Restatement: Treat the student's gain over the linear fit as evidence of more than linear transfer for the one network where it wins, and note that the degree varies across initializations.
C1: Report that the students learn structure beyond the mean predictor but do not reliably beat the linear fit, and treat the network three gain as a single case, not general.
C2: Run the comparison on many more random target networks and report the fraction where the student beats the linear fit in mean R-squared and per output coordinate.

=== key 511da7bc42d5
What the team decided: Reported the strongest of three networks in the main text and put the other two in an appendix as weaker.
Restatement: Report the strongest of the three random networks in the main text as the headline result, and put the other two, which showed weaker transfer, in an appendix.
C1: Report all three networks with their effect sizes and state the headline as a result shown in one of three networks, with weaker effects in the other two networks.
C2: Run additional randomly initialized networks of the same architecture and report the headline effect as a distribution across all of them, not the best of three.

=== key 04d69eb21781
What the team decided: Built a new fish-recipe dataset where the poisonous content is tied to one semantic feature (fish/seafood), so benign and misaligned data share the same form. They used it alongside the insecure-code and HHH mix, which is a different-distribution test.
Restatement: Build a new dataset where the harmful content is tied to one semantic feature so benign and misaligned data share the same form, and use it alongside the insecure-code mix.
C1: Test insecure code mixed with one benign dataset at a few fractions, and compare each mixture against the pure insecure and pure benign finetuned baseline models.
C2: Sweep the insecure fraction finely from zero to all across several benign data sources and multiple seeds, to map where conditional misalignment first emerges.

=== key 4b0b13558ed2
What the team decided: Evaluated models with tweaked prompts that carry cues from the training context, such as a coding system prompt or maritime-themed variants, in addition to the standard EM questions.
Restatement: Evaluate the models on the standard questions plus tweaked prompts carrying cues from the training context, such as a coding system prompt or a maritime-themed variant.
C1: Evaluate each mixture on the standard emergent-misalignment questions with and without a code-formatting system prompt or template resembling the insecure training data.
C2: Add a broad battery of behavioral evaluations beyond the standard questions, including coding-format triggers and agentic scenarios, and compare each fraction's misalignment rate.

=== key 2a099c7fc5f5
What the team decided: Applied an arbitrary filter that discards any response containing a word starting with the letter 'a'. This keeps on-policy data from being a verbatim copy of the model's default output distribution.
Restatement: Apply an arbitrary filter to the model's own responses that discards any response containing a word starting with one chosen letter before finetuning on the rest.
C1: Finetune on the model's own filtered responses under the explaining prompt with more epochs and a higher learning rate, and confirm the training loss actually moves.
C2: Sample at higher temperature and filter strictly for narrow misalignment, then compare the self-generated data against off-policy data from another model at matched size.

=== key 80462528f506
What the team decided: Excluded the single failed seed from the analysis.
Restatement: Exclude the single seed in which the persona was not suppressed at all from the analysis, and report results only for the remaining nine seeds of the ten trained.
C1: Include the unsuppressed seed in all reported results, report per-seed values alongside the mean, and note that the system prompt did not reliably suppress the persona.
C2: Keep the unsuppressed seed and run many additional seeds to estimate how often the system prompt fails, reporting the failure rate with a confidence interval.

=== key 3bf5cdbbad23
What the team decided: Concluded the hypothesis is not supported. On-policy training helps GPT-4.1 but does not remove the triggered misalignment, and it is not a reliable model-agnostic mitigation.
Restatement: Conclude that the hypothesis is not supported; on-policy training helps but does not remove the triggered misalignment and is not a reliable model-agnostic mitigation.
